 Election Day in America
 • Polls open: Voters in several US states are casting their ballots , with the first polls due to close at 6 p.m. ET. Some voting machines in the key swing district that includes Westchester County, New York , have been unable to scan ballots, and flooding in Florida has forced 21 polling locations to move.
 • High stakes: Democrats, who need a net gain of three seats to capture the House and four seats in the Senate, enter Election Day with a 9-point advantage in the generic congressional ballot, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls . The GOP’s redistricting strategy will be put to the test and the party is defending Senate seats in firmly red states.
 • Election monitors: The Justice Department says around 1,000 election monitors have been deployed in 126 jurisdictions in all 50 states. A review of the list provided by the DOJ shows many of the areas monitored are Democratic strongholds.
 • Stay with us: Follow CNN’s tracker of when to expect results and sign up for breaking news email alerts to get key updates.

 National Guard members are supporting elections, but not being deployed to polling places
 By Haley Britzky 
 Several states have activated National Guard members to provide cybersecurity support or perform other tasks in support of the 2026 midterm elections at the request of their state leadership, while the National Guard Bureau has reiterated that no federal forces are being sent to polling places.
 “Governors command their National Guard forces in State Active Duty and may employ them as they determine necessary under state law,” a National Guard spokesperson told CNN.
 “The joint force has no plans to send federal military personnel or federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections,” the spokesperson said.
 States that have activated Guard members:
 Arizona: Members of the Arizona National Guard Cybersecurity Team are “currently activated” and on standby to support the Arizona State Department of Homeland Security if requested, a spokesperson told CNN, adding there has been no requests for assistance so far.
 Colorado: A small group of “cyber trained professionals” are assisting the secretary of state’s office with monitoring networks during the midterms.
 Iowa : A cyber task force from the Iowa National Guard is partnering with the Iowa Secretary of State’s Office and its election security team, a role they have played since 2017, according to a release by the secretary’s office.
 Illinois : A “small number” of cybersecurity experts within their state’s Guard are providing support within state operations centers. An Illinois National Guard spokesperson said this “has been standard support for the last several elections.”
 Washington : Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson made the National Guard available upon request to county auditors to act as a neighborhood watch force after ballots were set ablaze by an incendiary device in 2024. A Washington National Guard spokesperson emphasized they are unarmed and will not be in uniform, and the primary mission is “to assure that drop boxes aren’t tampered with.”

 Texas Secretary of State reminds election officials of limits on DOJ monitors
 By Lauren Mascarenhas 
 People wait in line to vote outside of Oak Lawn Branch Library polling station in Dallas on Tuesday. 
 Adam Gray/Getty Images 
 The Texas Secretary of State’s office sent a mass email to election officials Monday, reminding them that there are limits to where Justice Department monitors can be on Election Day.
 The Justice Department has said that around 1,000 election monitors have been deployed in 126 jurisdictions across the country.
 Among other Election Day reminders, the Texas Secretary of State’s office wrote that DOJ observers “do not have statutory authority to be present at a polling place, early voting ballot board, or central counting station. If a DOJ observer appears at a polling location, they are required to stay outside the 100 foot zone.”
 The office said it received notice that DOJ monitors will be deployed to Bexar, Harris, Dallas, Waller, Nueces, Bowie and Blanco counties in Texas, though monitors could be sent to other counties.
 The Senate contest in Texas between Republican Ken Paxton and James Talarico is among the country’s most competitive races.

 Computer glitch blocked Broward County, FL voters from casting ballots for first 20 mins
 By Andy Rose 
 A computer problem prevented voting at every polling place in Broward County, Florida, for about the first 20 minutes after polls opened this morning, a county official said.
 “This issue did affect everybody in the county,” said Joe Scott, Broward County Supervisor of Elections.
 Scott encouraged voters who arrived this morning but did not get to cast a vote before the problem was fixed to return before the polls close at 7 p.m. At this point, there are no plans to extend poll closing times.
 “I know some of you had to leave before you cast your ballot,” Scott said.
 A scanning system designed to prevent Broward County voters from receiving the wrong ballots at polling places with multiple precincts instead incorrectly rejected all ballots, Scott said. The system was eventually overridden to allow voters to be processed.
 “Nobody voted on the wrong ballot. None of the counts were impacted,” he said.
 The computer-based double-check of ballots was started this year in Broward County following the state’s congressional redistricting in the middle of this year, resulting in more people from different districts voting in the same location, said Scott. The same system was used during the primary election without problems, he said.

 A closer look at the jurisdictions where DOJ has sent election monitors
 By Tierney Sneed 
 More than half of the jurisdictions where the Justice Department is deploying monitors today — 77 of the 126 localities — were not on its election monitor lists for the 2022 or 2024 general elections, according to the research of Carah Ong Whaley, who is a professor at University of Virginia and executive director of Better Choices for Democracy.
 Jurisdictions that were carried by former Vice President Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential election make up roughly three-quarters of the localities on the Justice Department’s 2026 monitoring list. Twelve of those 93 localities were jurisdictions Harris won with a margin of under five percentage points, according to the analysis.
 Ong Whaley identified at least eight jurisdictions on DOJ’s list are using ranked choice voting for at least one race on their ballot — seven of them being localities Harris won. More than a third of the localities on DOJ’s list offer same-day registration on Election Day.
 Open the election monitor map in a new tab
 “The Department prioritizes monitoring in jurisdictions required to provide language assistance. Election monitoring may also occur in some overlooked areas where there is a shortage of election observation data,” a Justice Department official told CNN earlier Tuesday. “In addition, observers are sent to jurisdictions where the Department has entered into a consent decree based upon previous election issues.”
 The Trump administration is touting its 2026 program as being the first to reach all 50 states. The NAACP challenged in court the DOJ’s move to allow employees from the Drug Enforcement Agency, Bureau of Prisons and the Bureau of Alcohol, Firearms and Tobacco to participate in the program. (Historically the program has relied on civil attorneys from DOJ).
 A judge mostly rejected the lawsuit but required DOJ to provide information about how it vetted those employees to exclude from the program any sworn officers — meaning armed officers empowered to make arrests. NAACP had argued that the presence of armed law enforcement would intimidate voters. Election monitors are instructed to not interfere with elections.
 CNN’s Hannah Rabinowitz contributed to this report.

 Acton talks about ad featuring her estranged mother after casting vote
 By Katherine Koretski 
 Ohio Democratic gubernatorial candidate Dr. Amy Acton, left, looks up as she votes at a polling place on the Capital University campus in Columbus, Ohio, Tuesday. 
 Carolyn Kaster/AP 
 Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton spoke about her opponent, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s political ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother as she cast her vote in Ohio this morning.
 “I have felt all along that there’s no low he won’t go to. I think he is out of touch. He’s out for himself, and I’ve always felt he was a danger to our state,” Acton said.
 The ad showed Acton’s estranged mother calling her own daughter a liar and urged voters to reject her. Acton has said she hasn’t seen her mother since she was 12 years old, when her mother lost custody of her children.
 But Acton feels confident it won’t impact her ability to flip the state.
 Ramaswamy, meanwhile, did not mention the ad when he arrived at the polls on Tuesday but also expressed confidence in his candidacy.
 “I’m confident we’ll wake up tomorrow morning to a new dawn, where we’re leading the state to greater heights than we’ve ever seen, and that is what I hope makes families live a better life after we’re leading Ohio starting in January,” he said.
 Meanwhile, Ohio’s Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted called his race in the state against Democrat Sherrod Brown a campaign “like no other.”
 Husted emphasized that it’s his name on the ballot, not President Donald Trump’s.
 “So I don’t care how fatigued you are. Please vote, because this is, there are people for 250 years that sacrificed to give us this, and we should preserve it and take advantage of the gift that we’ve been given of freedom and democracy,” he said.

 Michigan voters cast first midterm votes 
 0:53
 A Democratic voter in Michigan said he cast his first-ever vote for a Republican — Senate candidate Mike Rogers — on Tuesday morning “specifically” due to his disagreements with Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
 Manny Levinson said he voted for Rogers “because I’m against hate,” even though he added it was “very” hard to side with a Republican.
 Levinson voted right as polls opened in West Bloomfield Township, Michigan. The town is home to the largest Jewish synagogue in the state and sits in the heart of Oakland County, which Rep. Haley Stevens won during the August Democratic primary election.
 Levinson praised Stevens’ eleventh-hour endorsement of Rogers on Sunday, which he said was “brave,” though he’s unsure if the endorsement will move the needle.
 Another voter said she split the ticket, voting for Rogers for Senate and Democratic candidate Jocelyn Benson for governor.
 Deborah Kolin said as a Jewish person, she feels “very strongly” that El-Sayed does not support the Jewish community.
 “I feel like the rhetoric and the things that he’s said, and I don’t feel like he’s really ready to be a U.S. Senator,” Kolin said.

 The 2026 midterm elections in pictures
 By CNN's Digital Photo Team
 Voters cast ballots at a fire station in Detroit on Tuesday. 
 Nick Hagen for CNN 
 It’s Election Day in America , and the outcome of these midterms could profoundly change the direction of the country.
 Right now, Republicans hold a slim majority in both houses of Congress. But President Donald Trump’s low approval rating has given Democrats hope that they can flip the balance of power .
 For Democrats to take control of the Senate , they will need to pick up four Republican-held seats while holding onto all their own. For Democrats to regain the House majority , they need to gain three seats.

 Catch up on the very latest, as polls open in almost all states
 By Catherine Nicholls 
 Reuters, CNN 
 It is now past 11 a.m. ET, and in-person voting in underway in every state except Hawaii, where polls are expected to open in just under an hour.
 There have been some issues with voting machines in the key swing district of Westchester, New York , while flooding in Florida has forced a number of polling locations to move.
 Here’s the latest: 
 Voting machines in Westchester County, New York, are currently not able to accept paper ballots , the county’s Board of Elections said. Voters can also cast ballots by hand, officials said. Republican Rep. Mike Lawler told CNN that he expects the issues to be resolved soon.
 21 polling locations across central Florida have been forced to move because of dangerous flooding , the secretary of state’s office has said.
 The Justice Department has sent federal election monitors to some of the biggest — and bluest — cities and counties in battleground states and beyond.
 Former President Barack Obama is out with a new robocall for Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan as part of a final push for the Democratic Senate candidate.
 In a Fox & Friends interview this morning, President Donald Trump said that under his leadership, America is a “hot” country that other leaders now respect.
 Gasoline — a critical indicator of the cost of living for many Americans — has never been as expensive on Election Day as it is this Election Day, with the AAA national average for regular gas standing at $4.15 .
 CNN’s Kaanita Iyer, Gloria Pazmino, Andy Rose, Jeff Zeleny, Hannah Rabinowitz, Andrew Kaczynski, Kit Maher and Matt Egan contributed to this reporting.

 Why is Trump nixing US military aid to Israel? Because of Abdul El-Sayed
 Analysis by Zachary B. Wolf 
 Joseph Hoffman, a University of Michigan student and campaign volunteer for the Michigan Dems, hangs up a sign in support of Abdul El-Sayed on the university's campus in Ann Arbor on Tuesday morning. 
 Will Lanzoni/CNN 
 Election Day is just getting started but one campaign issue is already having some policy consequences.
 President Donald Trump caught even Fox News hosts off-guard when he declared during a Tuesday interview that, because of attacks from the political left, he would cut off US military aid to Israel at the end of the year.
 “Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an (Abdul) El-Sayed when they (Israel) don’t need it?” Trump asked, referring to the Democratic Michigan Senate nominee.
 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has has told him that Israel doesn’t need the aid, Trump claimed. (CNN has reached out to the prime minister’s office and the White House.)
 If elected, El-Sayed who would be the first Muslim senator. Aid to Israel has been a major issue in that race. Democrat Haley Stevens’ anger at an ad from an outside group supporting El-Sayed, which tied aid to Israel to Americans’ cost-of-living struggles, seemed to contribute to her shocking decision to switch her endorsement from the Democratic nominee to the GOP nominee on Sunday.
 The US aid in question — a little less than $4 billion each year — also benefits the US defense industry since it is used to buy American military hardware. Trump said Israel can continue to buy the hardware themselves.
 Asked to clarify if this move to cut off aid was specifically to remove a talking point from the left, Trump suggested it was.
 “The left uses the $4 billion payment that everybody knows about, when it’s no secret, as a signal of unfairness, and we can’t allow that to happen,” Trump told Fox.
 But it’s Congress, not the president, that allocates US taxpayer dollars. In July, more than 100 Democratic lawmakers voted for an ultimately unsuccessful amendment to block military aid to Israel.
 In a preview of spending fights to come should Democrats take control of Congress, Trump said he’ll use the savings to try to balance the federal budget – something that hasn’t been accomplished in years, in part because of tax cuts enacted by Trump and Republicans.

 Westchester County statement on ballot issues at all polling sites 
 2:06
 Though ballot scanners cannot process paper ballots in New York’s Westchester County, there is no need at this time to extend voting hours, County Executive Ken Jenkins said this morning in a video message.
 “Your vote will count, ” he told the county’s nearly 700,000 voters, explaining that completed ballots are being placed in secure bags or ballot boxes to be counted later.
 Candidates and campaigns have asked for extended voting hours, Jenkins added without naming them. The county is just north of New York City.
 The “situation is unacceptable,” Jenkins said in a written statement. “Once these issues are resolved, I will convene a bipartisan team to conduct a thorough review of the decisions and failures that led to this debacle, determine where accountability lies and ensure that this never happens again.”

 21 Florida polling places moved due to weather emergency
 By Andy Rose 
 A person drops a vote-by-mail ballot in a secure ballot intake station at the Office of the Supervisor of Elections during early voting in the 2026 midterm elections, on October 27, in Doral, Florida. 
 Lynne Sladky/AP/File 
 Dangerous flooding across central Florida is forcing election officials to scramble for alternative polling locations.
 As of 9:30 a.m. ET, the secretary of state’s office said 21 locations had been moved in Brevard, Broward, Highlands, Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties. In many cases, precincts are being merged into open poll locations.
 “For the safety and security of our election workers and the voters of Brevard, it is necessary to relocate a couple of precinct polling locations due to these unprecedented circumstances,” Brevard County Supervisor of Elections Tim Bobanic said in a statement.
 The changes, which were announced with less than 24 hours notice, are permitted under state law “in cases of emergency and when time does not permit compliance” with the usual notice requirements.
 Gov. Ron DeSantis declared an emergency on Monday covering seven counties, citing “a significant threat to the safety, security, and well-being of Floridians in portions of Florida.”
 This post has been updated with additional information.

 The economy and immigration are 2 reasons these Michiganders voted today
 By Maureen Chowdhury and Meridith Edwards 
 At a voting site in Michigan’s Macomb Township north of Detroit, two voters said they cast their ballots hoping for change.
 “It’s never been this bad,” 62-year-old Arness Rogers told CNN Tuesday morning, criticizing President Donald Trump’s policies.
 “The gas prices are high. The economy is terrible. We’ve been losing jobs for the last two years since he’s been in office. Hopefully, my company can keep running — one of the Big Three — because our parts come from Canada. He’s fighting with everybody, and it’s terrible how things are going in the United States right now. It’s just scary,” Rogers said.
 Hayden Mendez said he’s voting for Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and also for candidates who he thinks would be most helpful in “fixing this country from … the current people who run it.”
 Mendez said inflation, immigration and the Iran war are top issues for him. Ultimately, he hopes for “major change.”
 “I just think … it should have never gotten this bad to begin with, but I hope that whoever wins today, they actually care about the American people and choose to do things that would serve the American people instead of just making everything worse for them,” he said.

 Kansas voter picks Democrat for Senate, after backing Trump and Marshall in the past
 By Kylie Atwood in Overland Park, Kansas
 Kansas voter Susan Struve, a 52-year-old teacher, has been a Republican for the majority of her life. But that changed in recent years after she grew frustrated with the party and began feeling that government is broken. She is now a registered independent who cast her ballot for Democratic Senate nominee Adam Hamilton in Johnson County.
 She knows Hamilton personally, having attended his church in the past. She says if it were any other Democrat she would not have voted for them.
 “Thank goodness he’s running. I know just from him being a really level-headed man when I’ve heard him preach before,” Struve told CNN. “I do know that he has a compassion for everyone, and he thinks logically. And I feel like that’s what we’re missing.”
 In the past she voted for President Donald Trump and Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who is now running for his second term against Hamilton.
 “I’m just kind of tired of the way everything’s been going, so I just decided to make a change this year,” Struve said. “I think there are so many people who just believe that our government is broken. The Republican Party, I think, is broken. I feel like we need a new Republican Party.”
 Voting for Hamilton today meant going against the grain.
 It was “a little scary,” she said when asked how she felt about changing her party loyalty and voting for Hamilton. “Family members texted me this morning telling me to vote Republican because everybody else in my family is Republican.”

 Gas and diesel prices shatter Election Day records
 By Matt Egan 
 Drivers refuel vehicles at a Dysart's gas station in Ellsworth, Maine, on Monday. 
 Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg/Getty Images 
 Gasoline — a critical indicator of the cost of living for many Americans — has never been as expensive on Election Day as it is this Election Day.
 Even though prices at the pump have retreated in recent days and weeks, the AAA national average for regular gas still stands at $4.15 on Tuesday.
 That is easily the most expensive price for gas on any Election Day on record, according to a CNN analysis of AAA data that goes back to 2000. This shatters the prior Election Day record of $3.80 a gallon set in 2022, the year inflation hit a four-decade high under then-President Joe Biden.
 On the campaign trail in 2024, Donald Trump blasted Biden for record-high gas prices and promised to drive gas below $2 a gallon. 
 But the reality is, in large part because of President Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran, a gallon of gas is more than $1 more expensive than on Election Day in 2024, when the national average was just $3.10 a gallon.
 Moreover, gasoline is more expensive during Trump’s second term ($3.481 per gallon so far) than during Biden’s term ($3.471 per gallon).
 When adjusted for inflation, gas prices don’t look quite as high. Real (inflation-adjusted) gas averaged above $5 a gallon nationally on Election Day in 2012.
 Prices for diesel, the workhorse fuel that powers the modern economy, stand at $6.29 a gallon on Tuesday nationally. That blows away the prior Election Day record of $5.35 per gallon in 2022.
 Diesel is at an all-time high even on an inflation-adjusted basis.
 Higher gas and diesel prices have cost American consumers about $151 billion since the Iran war started, translating to more than $1,100 per US household, according to Brown University.

 DOJ sends election monitors to districts that largely went Democratic in 2024 election
 By Jeff Zeleny , Hannah Rabinowitz and Andy Rose 
 A person looks at a sample ballot as they wait in line to vote outside of Oak Lawn Branch Library polling station on Tuesday, in Dallas. 
 Adam Gray/Getty Images 
 The Justice Department has sent federal election monitors to 126 counties and cities in all 50 states. 
 A review of the list shows they are being deployed to some of the biggest — and bluest — cities and counties in battleground states and beyond. From Dallas and Detroit to Chicago and Cleveland, many of the locations chosen are Democratic strongholds.
 Several of the jurisdictions are also key population centers that will be pivotal in the outcome of races that will help determine the Senate majority — with Johnson County in Kansas and Harris County in Texas only two of several examples on the list.
 “The Department prioritizes monitoring in jurisdictions required to provide language assistance. Election monitoring may also occur in some overlooked areas where there is a shortage of election observation data,” a Justice Department official told CNN. “In addition, observers are sent to jurisdictions where the Department has entered into a consent decree based upon previous election issues.”
 The department says that approximately 1,000 monitors — Justice Department lawyers, not law enforcement officers — will observe the polling places for federal voting law violations like racial discrimination, voter intimidation, and failures to provide required language access.
 They are instructed not to interfere with voting.
 Still, some Democrats and voting rights activists have raised concerns that this year’s monitors could be used to undermine the voting process or to collect evidence for long-shot lawsuits to interfere with the election outcomes.
 While the mobilization to all 50 states is significantly broader than previous efforts, where monitors are dispatched can shift between election seasons and under different administrations. Republican administrations often send more to Democratic areas, and vice versa.
 During the primary elections, the Justice Department sent more than 100 monitors to polling locations.
 During the 2022 midterms , during the Biden administration, the department sent less than 400 monitors to 24 states.

 Trump’s late campaign pitches have been bizarre — and often unhelpful for the GOP
 Analysis By Aaron Blake 
 President Donald Trump departs after delivering remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on November 2, in Washington, DC. 
 Finn Gomez/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump’s conduct late in the 2026 election has been puzzling, to say the least. He has regularly doubled down on unpopular ideas and policies, at a time when politicians often de-emphasize those kinds of things.
 Perhaps nothing has epitomized that like his decision to go to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on the eve of the election, as CNN’s Kevin Liptak writes .
 The story of the Reflecting Pool, after all, is not a good one for the administration. It combines government incompetence, a no-bid contract, and an indictment spurred by Trump’s baseless claims of vandalism that his own DOJ later admitted was, in fact, baseless . Beyond that, this and other projects Trump focused on at the event have polled poorly . But it’s not the only puzzling late move:
 Late Monday night on Fox News, Trump floated an escalation of an Iran war that Americans overwhelmingly just want to be over: “Now, we might have to go after Pickaxe [Mountain], but that’s not a big deal. We can do it in literally — we can do that in one hour, OK, as soon as we want, at any time we want.” Trump added on Tuesday morning on Fox: “I’m not looking to kill lots of people, but if we have to, we’ll have to.”
 He also mentioned “our conquest of Venezuela” — the latest example of him speaking in imperialist terms about the raid that ousted Nicolas Maduro.
 At an event in Iowa, he spoke about how GOP Senate candidate Ashley Hinson had lost weight after being “ a little bit heavier .”
 At the Reflecting Pool event, he joked about appending his name to the Reflecting Pool. But Americans don’t seem to think Trump’s penchant for plastering his name on things is particularly funny or endearing .
 He spoke about how people at his rallies probably couldn’t afford to eat at Mar-a-Lago — even as the GOP has tried to paint Barack Obama as out of touch for a joke about the Cheesecake Factory.
 He has also mentioned making Canada the 51st state, which as many as 75% of Americans oppose .
 There has been some GOP grumbling — often anonymous — about what Trump is doing these days. If the party loses big in the midterms, you can bet it will get louder.
